:step/content.:tutorial/content:
We know how to integrate $e^x,$ but how do we integrate a function like $e^{2x}?$

The answer is to use a substitution. If we let $u=2x,$ then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x = \dfrac 1 2 \textrm d u.
$$

Now, we can write our original integral in terms of the new variable $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{u}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

After solving an integral using substitution, we should always double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2x}+C) & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{2x})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {e}^{2x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x)+0 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2x}\cdot 2 \\  & ={e}^{2x}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
If we let $u=1-3x,$ then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = -3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x = -\dfrac 1 3 \textrm d u.
$$

Then, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {e}^{1-3x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{u}\cdot (-\frac{1}{3})\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{u}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{1-3x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Integrating the Exponential Function With a Linear Exponent

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
If we let $u=5+4x,$ then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 4\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x = \dfrac 1 4 \textrm d u.
$$

Then, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {3}^{5+4x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {3}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int {3}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{{3}^{u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+C \\  & =\frac{{3}^{5+4x}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Integrating a General Exponential Function With a Linear Exponent

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
If you're comfortable with memorizing formulas, then it's worth noting that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {e}^{px+q}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{p}{e}^{px+q}+C, \\ \int {a}^{px+q}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{p\operatorname{ln}a}{a}^{px+q}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

If you don't like to memorize formulas, you can always use substitution to solve these types of integrals.
